en: The Heart Sutra of the Perfection of Wisdom, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Prajñā of Kaśmīra together with Lìyán and others.
Thus have I heard: At one time the Buddha was staying on Vulture Peak Mountain in the city of Rājagṛha, together with...
Together with a great assembly of bhikṣus and a multitude of bodhisattvas, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, immediately entered a samādhi called "Vast and Profound.

At that time, within the assembly, there was a bodhisattva mahāsattva named Avalokiteśvara. While practicing the profound Prajñāpāramitā, he clearly perceived that the five aggregates are all empty, and thereby transcended all suffering and distress.
Thereupon, Śāriputra, receiving the Buddha’s majestic power, joined his palms in reverence and addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, saying:
“O Son of Good Family!
"If there are those who wish to practice the profound perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*),
how should they cultivate it? Having asked this,
the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara then addressed the Venerable Śāriputra, saying:

“Śāriputra! When a son of good family or a daughter of good family practices the practice of the profound perfection of wisdom, they should contemplate that the nature of the five aggregates is empty.”
Śāriputra! Form is not different from emptiness; emptiness is not different from form.
Form is itself emptiness; emptiness is itself form.
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also like this.
Śāriputra, these dharmas have the characteristic of emptiness: they are neither born nor extinguished, neither defiled nor pure, neither increasing nor decreasing.

Therefore, in emptiness there is no form, no sensation, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; no eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind; no forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or phenomena; and no眼界 (eye-element) up to and including no意識界 (consciousness-element).
There is no ignorance, nor is there the extinction of ignorance; and so on, up to: there is no old age and death, nor is there the extinction of old age and death.
There is no suffering, no origination, no cessation, and no path. There is no wisdom, nor is there any attainment.
Because there is nothing to be apprehended, the Bodhisattva, by relying on the Prajñāpāramitā, has no hindrance in the mind.
Because there is no hindrance, there is no fear; being far removed from perverted dreams and delusions, one attains ultimate Nirvāṇa.
The Buddhas of the three periods rely on the Prajñāpāramitā and thereby attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

Therefore, know that the Prajñāpāramitā is the great divine mantra, the great illuminating mantra, the unsurpassed mantra, and the unequaled mantra; it is able to eliminate all suffering, for it is true and not false.
"Therefore, I proclaim the Prajñāpāramitā mantra.
He then spoke the mantra, saying:
"Tadyathā: gate gate pāragate pārasaṃgate bodhi svāhā. "Thus it is, Śāriputra!"
"All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, in their practice of the profound perfection of wisdom, should practice in this manner.
Having spoken thus,
the World-Honored One immediately arose from that vast and profound samādhi and praised the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!
Son of good family! It is so, it is so!"
It is as you have said.
The practice of the profound *prajñāpāramitā* should be practiced in this manner.
When one practices in this way, all Tathāgatas will rejoice in accordance with it.
When the Blessed One had spoken these words, the Venerable Śāriputra was filled with great joy, and the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara also rejoiced greatly.
At that time, the assembly of devas, humans, asuras, gandharvas, and others, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, were all greatly rejoiced; they believed, accepted, and practiced it accordingly.
The Heart Sutra of the Perfection of Wisdom (Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya-sūtra)
